lessons.title: Hydrogen and oxygen
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Chemistry — Non-metals: hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and ammonia, fertilisers, sulphur and sulphuric acid, chlorine and halogens (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the laboratory preparation and test of hydrogen.
Describe the laboratory preparation and test of oxygen.
Describe the combustion of elements in oxygen and classify oxides.
Use gas volume ratios in simple calculations.
reviewNotes: Gas volumes are compared at the same temperature and pressure (Avogadro's law).
Oxide classification: acidic (non-metal oxides such as CO₂, SO₂), basic (most metal oxides), amphoteric (Al₂O₃, ZnO) and neutral (H₂O, CO, NO).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Hydrogen
blocks.md: **Preparation**: zinc (or magnesium) + dilute hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. Collected over water or by upward delivery (it is the **least dense** gas). **Test**: a lighted splint gives a **squeaky pop**. Colourless, odourless, burns to form water: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. **Uses**: making ammonia (Haber process), hardening oils to make margarine, rocket fuel, cutting and welding (oxy-hydrogen).

blocks.title: Oxygen
blocks.md: **Preparation**: decomposing hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide as catalyst: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, collected over water. **Test**: a **glowing splint relights**. Elements burn in oxygen to form oxides: magnesium (bright white flame, MgO), sulphur (blue flame, SO₂), carbon (CO₂). **Uses**: respiration, hospitals, steel making, welding, rocket oxidiser.

blocks.title: Classes of oxide
blocks.md:
- **Basic oxides**: most metal oxides (MgO, CuO); react with acids to form salts; alkali if soluble.
- **Acidic oxides**: non-metal oxides (CO₂, SO₂, NO₂); react with alkalis; dissolve in water to form acids (SO₂ → acid rain).
- **Amphoteric**: react with both acids and alkalis (Al₂O₃, ZnO).
- **Neutral**: H₂O, CO, NO.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Hydrogen is explosive with air: always test small samples, away from flames.
- Manganese(IV) oxide is a catalyst: it is not used up.
- Carbon dioxide is an acidic oxide, but it is not a gas that supports burning.

blocks.caption: Apparatus to prepare a gas: reactants in a flask, gas passed along a delivery tube and collected over water in a gas jar.
blocks.alt: A conical flask connected by a delivery tube to an upside-down gas jar full of water in a trough.

blocks.title: Example 1 — gas volumes
blocks.statement: 10 cm³ of hydrogen is burnt in excess oxygen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (steam). What volume of oxygen reacts and what volume of steam forms (same temperature and pressure, above 100 °C)?
steps: Gas volumes are in the same ratio as the moles: H₂ : O₂ : H₂O = 2 : 1 : 2.
Oxygen used = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm³; steam formed = 10 cm³.
blocks.answer: 5 cm³ of oxygen; 10 cm³ of steam

blocks.title: Example 2 — oxygen from hydrogen peroxide
blocks.statement: What volume of oxygen at room temperature and pressure (24 dm³/mol) is obtained from 6.8 g of H₂O₂ (H 1, O 16)?
steps: Mr(H₂O₂) = 34; n = 6.8 ÷ 34 = 0.20 mol. Ratio H₂O₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1, so n(O₂) = 0.10 mol.

lessons.title: Nitrogen, ammonia and fertilisers
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Chemistry — Non-metals: hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and ammonia, fertilisers, sulphur and sulphuric acid, chlorine and halogens (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the properties and uses of nitrogen.
Describe the preparation, test, properties and uses of ammonia.
Explain the need for fertilisers and name common ones.
Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in fertilisers and describe environmental effects.
reviewNotes: N:P:K labels refer to nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium; the content values quoted are computed from formulae, not from product labels.
Fertiliser use in Cameroonian farming is mentioned in general terms; no statistics are given.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Nitrogen and ammonia
blocks.md: **Nitrogen** (N₂) makes up 78% of air; it is **unreactive** (strong triple bond), used to fill food packets and as liquid nitrogen coolant. **Ammonia** (NH₃): made in the lab by heating an ammonium salt with an alkali: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O + 2NH₃; dried with **quicklime** (CaO); collected by **upward delivery** (lighter than air). **Test**: turns damp red litmus **blue**. Very soluble in water, giving an alkaline solution; it reacts with acids to form **ammonium salts**: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl.

blocks.title: Fertilisers
blocks.md: Plants need **nitrogen (N)** for leaves and protein, **phosphorus (P)** for roots and **potassium (K)** for flowers and fruit. Fertilisers replace nutrients removed by crops. Common ones: **ammonium nitrate** NH₄NO₃, **ammonium sulphate** (NH₄)₂SO₄, **urea** CO(NH₂)₂ and **NPK** mixtures. Made by neutralising ammonia with acids. **Problem**: excess fertiliser washes into rivers and lakes (**eutrophication**): algae grow, then die and rot, using up oxygen so fish die.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Ammonia is lighter than air and very soluble: it cannot be collected over water or dried with concentrated sulphuric acid or calcium chloride (both react with it).
- Compare fertilisers by **% nitrogen** (mass), not by name.
- Do not store or apply fertilisers where they can run into drinking water.

blocks.caption: Percentage of nitrogen by mass in three fertilisers (computed from their formulae).
blocks.alt: A bar chart: ammonium sulphate 21.2 percent, ammonium nitrate 35 percent and urea 46.7 percent nitrogen.

blocks.title: Example 1 — % nitrogen in urea
blocks.statement: Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in urea, CO(NH₂)₂ (C 12, O 16, N 14, H 1).

blocks.title: Example 2 — which fertiliser?
blocks.statement: A farmer has 100 kg of ammonium nitrate (35% N) and 100 kg of ammonium sulphate (21.2% N). Which supplies more nitrogen and how much more?
steps: Nitrogen in ammonium nitrate = 100 × 0.35 = 35.0 kg; in ammonium sulphate = 100 × 0.212 = 21.2 kg.
Difference = 35.0 − 21.2 = 13.8 kg more from ammonium nitrate.

objectives: Describe sulphur and its burning to form sulphur dioxide.
State properties, uses and hazards of sulphur dioxide.

State properties and uses of dilute and concentrated sulphuric acid.
reviewNotes: Contact process conditions quoted: about 450 °C, vanadium(V) oxide catalyst and a pressure of about 1–2 atmospheres (typical textbook values).
Sulphur dioxide as a food preservative and bleach is mentioned generally; safe limits are not given.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Sulphur and sulphur dioxide
blocks.md: **Sulphur** is a yellow brittle non-metal; it burns in air with a blue flame to give **sulphur dioxide**: S + O₂ → SO₂. SO₂ is a colourless, choking, **acidic** gas that turns damp blue litmus red and **bleaches** coloured materials; it is a **reducing agent** (decolourises acidified potassium manganate(VII)). **Uses**: bleach for paper, food preservative, making sulphuric acid. **Harm**: causes acid rain and breathing problems.

blocks.title: The contact process
blocks.md:
1. Burn sulphur (or roast sulphide ores): S + O₂ → SO₂.
2. Convert to sulphur trioxide: **2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃** (exothermic) with **vanadium(V) oxide** catalyst at about **450 °C** and about 1–2 atmospheres.
3. Dissolve SO₃ in concentrated H₂SO₄ to make **oleum** (H₂S₂O₇), then add water to make H₂SO₄. (SO₃ is not added directly to water because the reaction is violent and makes a mist.)

blocks.title: Sulphuric acid
blocks.md: **Dilute** H₂SO₄: a strong acid (reacts with metals, bases, carbonates to give sulphates). **Concentrated** H₂SO₄: a **dehydrating agent** (turns blue copper(II) sulphate crystals white and sugar into black carbon), and generates a lot of heat with water: **always add acid to water**, never water to acid. **Uses**: fertilisers (ammonium sulphate), detergents, paints, **lead-acid car batteries**, cleaning metals.

blocks.title: Safety and watch out
blocks.md:
- Concentrated sulphuric acid causes severe burns; wear eye protection.
- Add the **acid to water slowly**, stirring.
- The catalyst does not change the equilibrium position; the compromise temperature gives a good rate and yield.

blocks.caption: The contact process: sulphur is burnt to SO₂, converted to SO₃ over a catalyst and made into sulphuric acid.
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows: sulphur, SO2, SO3 and sulphuric acid with conditions labelled.

blocks.title: Example 1 — acid from sulphur
blocks.statement: How much sulphuric acid (kg) could be made from 1000 kg (1 tonne) of sulphur if all the sulphur is converted? (S 32, H 1, O 16)
steps: S → SO₂ → SO₃ → H₂SO₄: 1 mol S gives 1 mol H₂SO₄. n(S) = 1 000 000 g ÷ 32 = 31 250 mol.

blocks.title: Example 2 — % sulphur
blocks.statement: Calculate the percentage of sulphur in sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄.

lessons.title: Chlorine, hydrogen chloride and the halogens
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Chemistry — Non-metals: hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and ammonia, fertilisers, sulphur and sulphuric acid, chlorine and halogens (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the preparation, properties, test and uses of chlorine.
Describe the properties of hydrogen chloride and hydrochloric acid.
Use silver nitrate to distinguish chloride, bromide and iodide ions.
Describe the importance of sodium chloride.
reviewNotes: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HOCl is the standard equation for chlorine water; HOCl is the bleaching/disinfecting species.
Chlorine is toxic: preparations must be a teacher demonstration in a fume cupboard.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Chlorine
blocks.md: A pale green, poisonous gas, denser than air. **Lab preparation** (teacher demonstration, fume cupboard): MnO₂ + 4HCl(conc) → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O (warm). **Test**: **bleaches damp litmus paper** (first red, then white). It reacts with metals: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃; with hydrogen to give HCl; with water: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HOCl; with cold sodium hydroxide: bleach (sodium chlorate(I)). **Uses**: **disinfecting drinking water and swimming pools**, bleach, making PVC and solvents.

blocks.title: Hydrogen chloride
blocks.md: HCl is a colourless gas, **very soluble** in water (forms **hydrochloric acid**, a strong acid), and makes white fumes with ammonia. It is made by reacting sodium chloride with concentrated sulphuric acid. **Sodium chloride** (common salt) is obtained from sea water (evaporation) or rock salt; it is used in food, preserving, and as a raw material: electrolysis of brine gives chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide.

blocks.title: Halide ions: silver nitrate test
blocks.md: Add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution: **chloride** gives a **white** precipitate (AgCl), **bromide** a **cream** precipitate (AgBr), **iodide** a **yellow** precipitate (AgI). The precipitates darken in light. Ionic equation: Ag⁺(aq) + X⁻(aq) → AgX(s).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Chlorine is poisonous: never smell directly; the gas is prepared only in a fume cupboard.
- Distinguish chlorine (Cl₂, gas) from chloride (Cl⁻, ion) and hydrochloric acid (HCl solution).
- Dry chlorine does not bleach dry litmus paper; the paper must be damp.

blocks.caption: Silver halide precipitates: silver chloride is white, silver bromide cream and silver iodide yellow.
blocks.alt: Three test tubes labelled chloride, bromide and iodide with white, cream and yellow precipitates.

blocks.title: Example 1 — iron in chlorine
blocks.statement: Hot iron wool burns in chlorine: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃. What volume of chlorine (24 dm³/mol) reacts with 5.6 g of iron (Fe 56)?

blocks.title: Example 2 — identifying a halide
blocks.statement: A solution gives a yellow precipitate with acidified silver nitrate. Which ion is present and what is the ionic equation?
steps: Yellow precipitate: iodide ions I⁻ (silver iodide).
